identification.title: All Glory Be to Christ
identification.notes: Words by Dustin Kensrue alone, set to the tune of Auld Lang Syne. Integrity Music and PraiseCharts both credit Kensrue as sole author; the Gospel Coalition lists the copyright as Dead Bird Theology and It's All About Jesus Music (ASCAP) and the recording as Kings Kaleidoscope's. Integrity lists CCLI 7008232. The list's guess of Kings Kaleidoscope is right for the recording churches know, but the writer is Kensrue (of Thrice, who also leads worship at his church), not the band. The album and the 2012 year come from the Gospel Coalition post; Integrity's page does not state a year. Reviewed as the song, not any one recording.

claims.structuralNotes: Three eight-line stanzas, each ending on the glory-to-Christ line, each followed by the same four-line chorus, sung once more at the close. Stanza one tells the proud planner that works fail unless the Lord builds and that life is a mist. Stanza two applies the Lord's Prayer petitions to Christ as bread of life and living water freely given, and invites hearers to come. Stanza three names Christ as the I Am, Faithful and True, the Lamb slain for sinners, who returns and makes all things new with God dwelling among his people. The chorus acclaims Christ as King forever. The voice is credal and exhortatory, declaring who Christ is and calling hearers to him; the resurrection is implied only.

claims.claim: Human works and legacy fail unless the Lord builds, and life is a vanishing mist; glory belongs to Christ.
claims.subject: God's sovereignty and the brevity of life

claims.claim: Christ is the bread of life and the living water freely given, and hearers are invited to come and feed on him.
claims.subject: Christ as provision and the invitation

claims.claim: Christ is the I Am, Faithful and True, the Lamb slain for sinners, who will return and make all things new, with God dwelling among his people.
claims.subject: Atonement, return and new creation

claims.claim: Christ is King, his reign is sung forever, and glory is his.
claims.subject: The kingship of Christ

strengths.title: Glory given to Christ as king
strengths.explanation: The chorus gives glory to Christ and acclaims his rule, and the verses place human striving beneath that. A congregation is made to sing who is worthy and who is not.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lamb who was slain is worthy of glory - the direction of the chorus's praise.

strengths.title: Mortality set beside the Lamb and the new creation
strengths.explanation: The song is honest about brevity and vanity, then names Christ as the Lamb slain for sinners who returns and makes all things new, with God dwelling among his people. Hope rests in what Christ does, not in the singer.
strengths.scriptureRationale: He makes all things new - the horizon of the last verse.

strengths.title: Christ as bread of life and living water
strengths.explanation: The second stanza applies the Lord's Prayer petitions to Christ himself, as the bread of life and the water freely given, and invites hearers to come to him. Provision and invitation are tied to Christ, not to the singer's effort.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Christ is the bread of life; whoever comes to him will not hunger.

doctrinesAffirmed: The kingship and worthiness of Christ
The deity of Christ as the I Am
The atoning death of Christ the Lamb
Christ's return and the renewal of creation
The brevity of life and the vanity of achievement apart from the Lord
Christ as the bread of life and living water
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. A hymn that sets human legacy against Christ's reign, applies the Lord's Prayer petitions to Christ as bread and water, and ends on the Lamb slain for sinners, his return and new creation. The atonement is stated, though briefly; the resurrection is implied rather than stated.

strengths.title: A familiar tune with new words
strengths.explanation: Set to Auld Lang Syne, the melody is already in most heads, so a room can sing the chorus on the first pass.

strengths.title: Suits New Year and thanksgiving
strengths.explanation: The theme of fleeting time against God's rule fits a year's end or a service of reflection.

communal.vocalRangeNote: The original recording is in E per Integrity's record; the tune is a familiar folk melody that sits comfortably for most rooms. No chart was read.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: One chorus returns after each stanza, and each stanza ends on the same glory-to-Christ line; the repetition means more each time since each stanza gives a further reason Christ is worthy.
communal.assessment: Congregational in voice and in tune. The folk-tune setting makes it easy to join and the plural voice keeps the room together. It fits a year's end, a thanksgiving service, or any set that wants a hymn-like sung confession of Christ's kingship.

strengths.title: Christ named outright
strengths.explanation: The chorus names Christ and acclaims him as king, so no one has to guess whom the praise is for.

clarity.assessment: Clear. The Lord's Prayer allusions and the Revelation imagery are familiar to a churchgoer, and the contrast between human legacy and Christ's reign is plain. Stanzas are dense but easy to learn.

synthesis.summary: A congregational hymn with new words to a familiar tune. It sets the brevity of human achievement against Christ's reign, offers Christ as bread of life and living water, names him the I Am and the Lamb slain for sinners who returns to make all things new, and closes each stanza on glory to Christ. Christ is named throughout. The resurrection is implied only. No false claims.

scriptureReferences.relevance: The kingdom and daily bread petitions of the Lord's Prayer - the second verse.
The Lamb is worthy of glory - the direction of the chorus.
God making all things new - the last verse's horizon.
Life as a mist that vanishes - the first verse's observation on brevity.
Christ the bread of life - the second stanza.
Unless the Lord builds, labour is vain - the first stanza.
